children.text: Bacarra Church is the parish church of Saint Andrew the Apostle in Bacarra, Ilocos Norte. Its best-known feature is the coral-brick bell tower, Torre ti Bacarra, whose dome collapsed in the 1983 earthquake. Just north of Laoag, it fits easily into a half-day outing.

The church's formal name is Saint Andrew the Apostle Parish, and it stands on M. Castro Street in Barangay Santa Rita, Bacarra, Ilocos Norte. It belongs to the Diocese of Laoag and is still an active church where Mass is held, not just a monument. Bacarra is the town directly north of the provincial capital, Laoag, so close that you reach it by crossing a single bridge.
The church is famous for the bell tower that stands apart from the main building. Locals call it Torre ti Bacarra. It is built of coral bricks and is said to be about

(160 ft) tall. Because the dome at the top is gone, it is nicknamed the "beheaded" or "acrobatic" bell tower. Tremors from 1931 to 1971 made the dome lean, and the 1983 Luzon earthquake is said to have toppled it completely.

The history goes back to early Spanish colonial times. According to Wikipedia, the Augustinians founded the town of Bacarra on September 18, 1590, and in 1593 built a church and convent on the spot where Bacsalandoc, the first settler and a chieftain, had built his hut. Bacarra became a visita of Laoag in 1603 and an independent parish in 1614, and a new church was inaugurated in 1782. Sources differ slightly on construction dates, so check the on-site information for exact years.

The church was declared a National Cultural Treasure on August 1, 1973, by Presidential Decree No. 260, and the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) also treats it as a National Historical Landmark. It is less famous than Paoay Church, so there are few tour groups and you can look around quietly. It makes a good extra stop on an Ilocos Norte church tour or a drive out of Laoag. For a first visit, look up at the tower from the churchyard first, then see the church interior and the museum. One to two hours is enough, and with extra time you can build a half-day route continuing to Laoag and Paoay Church. Once you know why the tower lost its roof, the same building becomes far more striking.

This freestanding three-story tower of coral bricks has a distinctive domeless silhouette that has become the church's symbol. Looking up from the yard beside the church, you can feel its height. Because it stands apart from the church, it is hard to fit both in one frame, but that also makes it a fine standalone monument.

blocks.title: The story of the roofless tower

children.text: Tremors from 1931 to 1971 made the dome lean, and the 1983 Luzon earthquake brought it down. It shows how Ilocos has lived with earthquakes over the centuries. Locally the tower is also said to be called the "acrobatic bell tower of Asia."

blocks.title: The old bell that still rings

children.text: According to a travel blog, the tower's original bell is still rung by pulling a rope. You may be able to hear it if you time your visit, so ask locally.
The Baroque-style church, inaugurated in 1782, serves as an active parish. Restoration after the 1983 earthquake is said to have been completed in 1984. Please be quiet and respectful during Mass.

The museum occupies the restored two-story convent from the Spanish colonial era. It is said to display religious artifacts, archival photos and documents, and cultural items donated by residents. Check opening hours locally.

Behind the old convent, an underground staircase and three tunnels were found, thought to lead toward the Bacarra River, the tower and the altar. Whether they are open to visitors is not known, so ask on site.
The NHCP announced plans to restore the tower in 2018, and the restored tower was turned over to the Diocese of Laoag in November 2020. Check the tower's current condition when you visit.
From central Laoag, take a jeepney or tricycle north to Bacarra. The two towns are only
a bridge apart
, so the ride is short.
Arrive at the churchyard and photograph the whole tower from below. The church faces northwest, and one blog suggests the afternoon light is better.
Step inside the church and quietly look around the altar and interior. Check first that you will not clash with a Mass.
Visit the Museo de Bacarra in the old convent to see religious artifacts and photo archives.
Have a light lunch in town, then return to Laoag.
If you prefer the afternoon, swap the order and arrive around 15:00 to catch the light on the church facade.

items.title: Afternoon photo route
items.subtitle: When the tower catches the light

children.text: Take a jeepney or tricycle from Laoag to Bacarra. It is a short ride, so there is no rush.
From the open space in front of the church, frame the northwest-facing facade together with the tower. Some say the afternoon light falls on the facade and gives good photos.
Walk up close to the tower to see the texture of the coral bricks and the broken top. Some remains nearby are said to lie buried in the ground.
Check whether the museum is open and, if so, drop in briefly.
Return to Laoag and have dinner in the city after sunset.
Check opening hours locally.
Domestic flights run from Manila (NAIA) to Laoag International Airport (LAO). Airlines and frequencies vary by season, so check the latest schedule.
From the airport to central Laoag you can take a tricycle or jeepney, and one travel guide lists fares around the airport at about
per person.
Long-distance buses run from Manila to Laoag, and the trip is closer to an overnight journey. Check operators and fares locally.
After arriving in Laoag, transfer to a jeepney or tricycle bound for Bacarra.
Bacarra is the town just north of Laoag, and a travel blog describes it as a short jeepney ride for the minimum fare. The straight-line distance is about
6 km
The exact boarding point and fare are best confirmed with locals in Laoag.
If you hire a tricycle for the day, you can combine Bacarra with Paoay, La Paz Sand Dunes and more. Negotiate the price.
Ilocos Norte is generally dry from November to April, which is good for walking around the outdoor church and tower. Since the church faces northwest, some suggest visiting in the afternoon.

June to October is the rainy and typhoon season, so rain can upset your plans. During Holy Week and the parish feast day, when Catholic events peak, there are many Masses and visits may be restricted, so check the latest announcements.

During the day, early morning is quiet and cool enough for walking, while the afternoon, when light reaches the church facade, is better for photos. Midday offers little shade and is especially hot from March to May. Check the weather and typhoon news for all of Ilocos Norte again right before you go.

Bacarra itself is a small town, so most visitors stay in Laoag. Laoag has hotels and guesthouses clustered together, making it a good base for visiting nearby churches, and it is easy to reach from the airport and bus terminals. Prices and availability vary by season, so confirm directly. During Holy Week and long weekends rooms fill quickly, so booking ahead is safer.

I recommend trying Ilocano food in Laoag. Vigan longganisa sausages, Ilocano-style empanada and pinakbet are available in city eateries and the market. In Bacarra you can grab something simple at small eateries near the church or at the market, so a light lunch there and a proper dinner in Laoag is an easy rhythm.
After the church, stop by a museum or plaza in Laoag. It helps you understand the history and culture of Ilocos Norte at a glance.
Visits are restricted during Mass, so check the Mass schedule before you arrive or ask a church staff member.
Because the church faces northwest, some say afternoon visits give better photos of the facade.
Dress modestly, covering shoulders and knees.
Museum hours may not be fixed, so check locally before a midday visit.
Combine it with Paoay Church and La Paz Sand Dunes from Laoag for a half-day to full-day route.
The tower is mainly seen from the outside, so ask locally before trying to climb it.
In the heat of March to May, bring a hat and water.
Ask the diocese office or your hotel staff in Laoag about Mass and museum hours before you go to avoid a wasted trip.
Take two tower photos, one wide from across the road and one looking up from its base, to show its scale.
This is an active church, so stay quiet during Mass and prayer and be considerate of others before taking photos.
Museum opening hours and fees could not be confirmed in this research. Check the latest announcements.
The tower's condition may change with repairs, and access could be restricted.
Construction dates differ between sources, so signs may say something different.
In the rainy season, typhoons and heavy rain can make travel difficult.
Agree on the fare before boarding a tricycle.
Sidewalks in town are narrow and vehicles pass by, so watch the road when taking photos.

The capital of Ilocos Norte lies just to the south and is the hub for lodging, restaurants and transport. It is a short ride away. Museums, a market and eateries are concentrated there, so it is a good stop before or after Bacarra.

A Baroque church known as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It is a good next stop heading south from Bacarra. You travel by car through Laoag, and comparing the two churches shows what is distinctive about Ilocos church architecture.
Desert-like sand dunes near Laoag where you can try sandboarding. After a church tour, an afternoon visit pairs well with the breeze and sunset.
A historic lighthouse on the northern coast, suited to a route continuing north from Bacarra. You can stop on the way toward Pagudpud.
